```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = requireNamespace("emmeans", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

## The problem

Adjusting p-values for the false discovery rate (FDR) with the
Benjamini-Hochberg procedure is common when many comparisons are made. In
'emmeans', this is done with `adjust = "fdr"`. However, FDR adjustments are
defined for tests, not for confidence intervals, so `confint()` replaces them
with a Bonferroni adjustment. The intervals are then more conservative than
the p-values, and the two can lead to different conclusions.

Consider the `chickwts` data (base R): chick weights after six weeks on six
feed supplements, giving 15 pairwise comparisons.

```{r setup}
library(fcrci)
library(emmeans)

fit <- lm(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts)
prs <- pairs(emmeans(fit, ~ feed), adjust = "fdr")
```

The FDR-adjusted p-values:

```{r}
test(prs)
```

And the confidence intervals of the same contrasts:

```{r}
confint(prs)
```

Note the footer: the intervals were adjusted with the Bonferroni method, the
only indication that the requested FDR adjustment was not applied to them. For
example, `horsebean - linseed` has an FDR-adjusted p-value of about 0.023, yet
its interval includes zero. A reader comparing the two tables would not know
whether that difference is significant.

## FCR-adjusted intervals

Benjamini and Yekutieli (2005) defined the false coverage-statement rate (FCR),
the interval counterpart of the FDR: the expected proportion of intervals that
fail to cover their parameter among the intervals reported for the selected
(significant) parameters. They showed that if $R$ of $m$ hypotheses are
rejected by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at level $q$, constructing
marginal intervals at confidence level

$$1 - \frac{R\,q}{m}$$

controls the FCR at level $q$ when the test statistics are independent.
Since the procedure
rejects exactly the hypotheses with $p_i \le Rq/m$, these intervals exclude
the null value exactly for the rejected hypotheses.

`confint_fcr()` applies this adjustment to an 'emmeans' object, reading the FDR
method from the `adjust` setting used to create it:

```{r}
res <- confint_fcr(prs)
res
```

Now `horsebean - linseed` has an interval that excludes zero, matching its
p-value, and `casein - meatmeal` (FDR-adjusted p = 0.057) has an interval that
includes zero. The footer reports the confidence level used, $1 - 11 \times
0.05 / 15 \approx 0.963$. The details are available with `fcr_info()`:

```{r}
fcr_info(res)
```

Because the intervals are computed by 'emmeans' itself (with
`adjust = "none"` and the FCR level), degrees of freedom, back-transformations
and one-sided intervals behave exactly as in 'emmeans'. The common shortcut
`emmeans(fit, pairwise ~ feed, adjust = "fdr")` also works: `confint_fcr()`
then uses its `contrasts` component.

## Ratios and families defined by `by` variables

The `pigs` data from 'emmeans' records the concentration of leucine in pigs
fed three protein sources at four protein percentages. On the log scale,
differences become ratios after back-transformation. Here each percentage is a
separate family of three comparisons, as in 'emmeans':

```{r}
fit2 <- lm(log(conc) ~ source * factor(percent), data = pigs)
prs2 <- pairs(emmeans(fit2, ~ source | percent), adjust = "fdr")
res2 <- confint_fcr(prs2, type = "response")
res2
```

Each family receives its own confidence level, depending on how many of its
hypotheses were rejected. An interval for a ratio excludes 1 exactly when the
FDR-adjusted p-value is at most 0.05. When a family has no rejections, the
level is computed with $R = 1$ (the Bonferroni level), so that no interval
excludes the null value. Benjamini and Yekutieli construct no intervals in that
case; this fallback is a convention of the package that keeps the table
complete.

```{r}
fcr_info(res2)
```

To treat all 12 comparisons as a single family, use `by = NULL`, as you would
in `summary()`:

```{r}
fcr_info(confint_fcr(prs2, type = "response", by = NULL))
```

## Dependent contrasts: the Benjamini-Yekutieli version

The FCR guarantee of Benjamini and Yekutieli (2005) for the level above
assumes independent test statistics. Contrasts estimated from the same model
are usually correlated, and t statistics that share a variance estimate are
dependent even when the estimates are not. If a guarantee under any dependence structure is required,
use the Benjamini-Yekutieli procedure, either through `adjust = "BY"` in
'emmeans' or with `method = "BY"`:

```{r}
fcr_info(confint_fcr(prs, method = "BY"))
```

The level now includes the factor $\sum_{i=1}^{m} 1/i$, which makes both the
p-values and the intervals more conservative. The intervals and p-values still
agree with each other.

## What the intervals mean

* For the significant contrasts, the intervals control the FCR (on average, at
  most a proportion $q$ of them fail to cover the true value) when the test
  statistics are independent (`"BH"`) or under any dependence (`"BY"`). For
  correlated contrasts with `"BH"`, this is not a formal guarantee.
* Intervals are also shown for the non-significant contrasts, so that the
  table is complete and consistent with the p-values. The FCR criterion makes
  no coverage statement about these intervals.
* A single, unadjusted 95% interval should not be read from this table; use
  `confint(prs, adjust = "none")` for that.

## Using the level elsewhere

`fcr_level()` works with any vector of p-values, so the same adjustment can be
applied to results from other packages, as long as the intervals and p-values
are based on the same test statistic:

```{r}
p <- c(0.0004, 0.003, 0.012, 0.04, 0.21, 0.67)
fcr_level(p, q = 0.05)
```

genes. *BMC Bioinformatics*, 12, 288.
